Consider carefully: if you only want to model and tune parameters, are unwilling to check data sources and permissions, find it hard to accept models being rejected by business or compliance teams, or are unwilling to invest time in documentation, reproduction and communication, the actual work will differ from your expectations.

The core outputs are reviewable analytical conclusions and reproducible models: data descriptions and quality records, reproducible code, baseline models and performance metrics, validation and error analysis, plans for monitoring bias and drift, and conclusions and limitations written in business language, rather than simply achieving a high model score.

Low-risk exploration: use public or fictional data to complete an exercise of writing a data description and quality checklist, building a baseline model with validation and error analysis, and writing conclusions and uncertainty statements in nontechnical language. Assess only your work preferences; the exercise involves no real business data or personal information and does not constitute successful job training, data authorization or a promise of employment.

Where are the boundaries between data scientists and adjacent analysis, statistics and operations research roles?

This table compares data scientists with adjacent business intelligence analysts, statisticians, operations research analysts, computer and information research scientists, mathematicians and bioinformatics scientists across seven dimensions: core purpose, main objects and governing criteria, core process, main outputs, responsibility holders, collaboration and supervision, and limits on conclusions. Adjacent roles all involve data and quantitative methods, but their objects—end-to-end data modeling and prediction, business metrics and reports, statistical inference and experimental design, operations optimization and decision models, computing and information science problems, and biomedical statistics—and whether building verifiable models from raw data is central do not transfer merely because the roles are adjacent. Compare actual outputs and business stages item by item.
Core purpose
Build and validate models from raw data, produce reviewable predictive or explanatory conclusions, and deliver and monitor them in business language.

Business intelligence involves queries/reports/trends and system testing; statisticians work on theory/sampling analysis; operations research develops options under constraints; computing research develops computational methods/systems; mathematicians work on theory and applications; bioinformatics scientists develop computational and statistical tools for biomolecular data. These purposes can overlap without automatically transferring responsibilities.
Main objects and governing criteria

Business problems, raw data and features, models and evaluation metrics, data permissions and compliance boundaries; governed by business objectives, methodological standards and the employer's information management policies.

Metrics and business information (business intelligence), statistical problems/survey data (statisticians), operational objectives and constraints (operations research), computing science problems (computing research), mathematical structures (mathematicians), and molecular information such as genomic/proteomic data (bioinformatics scientists). These are not mutually exclusive objects or authorization for clinical practice.
Core process
Define the problem → check data and permissions → clean and engineer features → model and compare → validate and analyze errors → deliver, monitor and iterate.

Adjacent fields may respectively involve reporting and trend testing, statistical analysis, optimization solving, computational algorithm research, mathematical proofs and applications, and bioinformatics computing tools and molecular data analysis. Processes may overlap; check the actual role.
Main outputs
Reproducible models and code, validation and error analysis, bias and drift monitoring plans, and business-facing conclusions and limitations.

Adjacent fields may deliver metrics/systems, statistical results, optimization plans, algorithm prototypes, mathematical methods, and bioinformatics tools/molecular data research analyses. Check specific responsibilities and approval authority against the role; these are not universally exclusive outputs of each occupation.
Responsibility holders

Practitioners are responsible for the reliability of methods and validation and for the scope and uncertainty of conclusions. Authorized personnel and business stakeholders decide data usage permissions, whether models go live and business decisions; practitioners do not decide these unilaterally.

Adjacent fields bear corresponding responsibility for the metrics, statistics, optimization, computing research or bioinformatics work actually assigned. Job titles do not confer personnel budget authority, clinical sign-off authority or system deployment rights.
Collaboration and supervision

Collaborate within authorized permissions with business stakeholders, data engineering and IT, product and operations, compliance and legal teams, reporting to a business lead or technical supervisor. When data is unavailable or ownership unclear, target leakage or sample bias occurs, model performance is abnormal, or compliance boundaries are unclear, pause high-risk actions, verify facts, preserve records and escalate under established policies.

Editorial collaboration checks: actual division of work among business, collection, operational decision-making, research engineering and biological research teams. Bioinformatics scientists focus on molecular information and computational tools; a universal reporting line across employers has not been verified.
Limits on conclusions

Compare main purposes and outputs without treating prediction/inference/optimization/reporting as mutually exclusive responsibilities. Data science may propose management plans, but titles do not imply approval authority. Business intelligence may also analyze/test systems; do not claim it never validates models.
Preparation levels and practice requirements for adjacent roles do not apply to this occupation; check official information for each occupation and the requirements of the specific role item by item.
Key professional judgments

Six recurring professional judgments: are the business problem and evaluation metrics clearly defined; have data sources, field meanings and usage permissions been checked; are data quality and sample representativeness sufficient to support conclusions; has the model been independently validated and checked for target and data leakage; are uncertainty and scope of applicability reported honestly; and when anomalies, bias or unclear compliance boundaries arise, is work paused, reviewed and escalated?

First interview stakeholders to identify the problem to analyze and translate business objectives into measurable evaluation metrics. A vague problem definition can divert all subsequent work from business needs.
Confirm data sources, field meanings, sampling definitions and usage authorization. Unauthorized data or unclear definitions create both compliance and methodological risks.

Use statistical software to clean and process raw data and assess missing values, anomalies and sample representativeness. Modeling without checking quality can misinterpret data problems as business patterns.

Test, validate and redesign models, compare metrics such as loss functions or the proportion of variance explained, and check for target leakage, data leakage and overfitting from tuning. A high score on the same dataset alone is not evidence of generalization.
Assessment four: is model validation sufficient?

Explain results using charts and business language and state confidence ranges, assumptions and scope of applicability. Presenting statistical results as certain conclusions misleads business decisions.
Assessment five: do conclusions explain uncertainty?

When data is unavailable or ownership unclear, performance drops significantly, bias or drift exceeds expectations, or compliance boundaries are unclear, pause deployment or high-risk actions, verify facts, preserve records and escalate under established policies.

Overtrusting automatically generated results
Code, features or conclusions from generative assistants may look complete but rest on incorrect assumptions or be unsuitable for the current data distribution.
Treat generated results as drafts awaiting validation, review methods and data assumptions through standard procedures, and independently validate and document key conclusions.
Data and target leakage

Using information unavailable at prediction time, including target-derived fields unavailable at prediction time, or involving test data in model selection/repeated tuning can make performance estimates overly optimistic, with new-data or deployment performance below evaluation results. Correlated features alone are not leakage; examples do not establish that all models fail to generalize or decline by a uniform amount.

Methodological suggestion: information unavailable at prediction time must not enter training. Split data first; fit preprocessing/feature selection only on training data, and do not use test data for model selection. Cross-validation can use Pipeline. Check time/group splits separately based on data dependencies; do not always split randomly.
Sample bias and unfairness

When training data fails to represent the target population, models may systematically overestimate or underestimate certain groups, causing material harm in finance, healthcare and human resources settings.

values: Fictional analytical scenario material (exercise input)

Fictional scenario: a data scientist encounters four problems within one project cycle. First, a field in training data is only available in the prediction period but has been used as a feature. Second, business stakeholders want a model for high-risk decisions deployed within two weeks. Third, evaluation metrics meet targets across the whole sample, but errors for one group are noticeably higher. Fourth, some data contains customers' personal information, and a colleague requests exporting raw data to an external tool for processing.
Supplied material: business problem and evaluation metrics; field descriptions and data dictionary; data usage and traceability requirements; model deployment and review procedures.

Missing material: rules for deciding whether the field constitutes leakage, whether validation scope may be reduced when time is short, authority for handling high bias, and whether personal information may be exported to external tools. If these conditions are needed in the exercise, state your assumptions and whom you need to consult explicitly.
Task requirements

Write a one-page handling and escalation plan covering assessment and handling of the suspected leakage field, communication and minimum validation requirements when time is short, a response route for high bias, and permissions and traceability when personal information is involved.

State which information comes from the scenario and which remains an assumption, and whether the basis is field descriptions and the data dictionary, validation standards or data security and compliance requirements.
Reference deliverable (deducible from the scenario)

The plan should include: suspected leakage field (check availability at prediction time, redo features and validation based on availability if needed, and record the rationale); insufficient time (explain risks through established procedures, specify indispensable validation steps, and suggest narrowing deployment scope or delaying if needed, without skipping validation to meet schedules); high bias (analyze group-level errors and identify causes, restrict use cases if needed and escalate approval through compliance procedures, retaining assessment records); personal information (process within authorized scope without exporting to external tools; where genuinely needed, apply under established policies and process through compliant channels); handover (state the status, actions taken and pending confirmations for all four matters).
The reference deliverable lists required elements only; wording need not match the example if the judgment rationale is explained.
Boundaries and conclusions that cannot be inferred

This exercise checks awareness of data availability and leakage assessment, minimum validation requirements, bias handling and data compliance only. It does not assess whether real workplace handling is compliant, nor constitute compliance, security or legal advice.

Do not use actual employer data or nonpublic business material. Real personal information and restricted data processing, model deployment and industry regulatory requirements must follow employer information management policies, data security and personal information protection rules, and industry compliance requirements; obtain corresponding authorization under current rules where needed.

items.title: Fictional exercise material: handling data leakage and bias

values: Day 1: read a public resource
Find a public introduction to data quality or model validation, mark three key requirements and corresponding practices, and record what you want to confirm.
Day 2: check fields and quality
Using public or fictional data, list field meanings, possible missing values or anomalies and checking methods.
Day 3: build a baseline model
Build a simple baseline using public or fictional data and state the split method and metrics used.
Day 4: write validation and error analysis
Explain how you validated, the main sources of error and whether leakage or bias risks exist.
Day 5: write conclusions and limitations
Write a one-page conclusion in nontechnical language, including applicable conditions, uncertainty and uses that are not recommended.
Day 6: let someone review using only the material
Ask a peer to review your judgments using only your plan, and record their questions.
Day 7: decide whether to continue
Return to this page's assessment checklist and write three reasons to continue and two conditions requiring caution.

entries: Concrete change: can you explain data evidence, validation order, bias and leakage judgments, and compliance response routes using the supplied material, rather than merely writing "handled"?
Facts and choices: would you rather focus on modeling and methods, business interpretation and implementation, or data and platform engineering?
Exercise demands: prolonged screen work, intensive cognitive effort and repeated challenges to conclusions—which step drains you most, and can you accept its recurrence at work?
Material boundaries: all exercise material is fictional or based on public data; do not include actual employer data or nonpublic business information.
Response to feedback: when business stakeholders or reviewers question your methods and conclusions, are you willing to return to validation and evidence?
Interest in the process: even when cleaning and validation are tedious, are you willing to complete documentation, reproduction and review every time?

Next step: if you want to continue after all six previous steps, complete a cycle from data checks and modeling through validation and interpretation under compliant conditions (such as a real project retrospective or probation task), and ask an experienced person to review it. If one step is particularly draining, narrow the track first and validate again.

entries.answer: Develop and implement techniques or analytical applications using data-oriented programming languages and visualization software to turn raw data into meaningful information: analyze, process or clean large datasets with statistical software; create charts or other visualizations to communicate analysis results; test, validate and redesign models to ensure accurate prediction of target outcomes; compare models using metrics such as loss functions or the proportion of variance explained; apply feature selection algorithms; identify relationships, trends or factors that may affect research outcomes; write new functions or applications in programming languages for analysis; interview stakeholders to identify problems to analyze; design surveys or other data collection instruments; report modeling and analysis results to management and other end users; and recommend data-driven solutions to key stakeholders. Dynamic data reports may also be created.

entries.answer: This occupation centers on building and validating models from raw data, producing reviewable predictive or explanatory conclusions, and delivering and monitoring them. Business intelligence analysts center on metric systems and report delivery; statisticians on inference methods and experimental design; operations research analysts on optimization and decision modeling; computer and information research scientists on algorithm and system research; mathematicians on developing and proving mathematical theories; and biostatisticians provide statistical methodological support for biomedical research. Similar names do not make duties, evaluation standards or qualifications interchangeable.

description.text: Data scientists (O*NET-SOC 15-2051.00) use data-oriented programming languages and visualization software to turn raw data into meaningful information. Tasks include analyzing and cleaning large datasets with statistical software, creating charts and other visualizations, testing, validating and redesigning models, comparing statistical model performance metrics, applying feature selection algorithms, identifying relationships, trends and influencing factors, writing new functions or applications for analysis, reading scientific articles to identify emerging analytical trends, interviewing stakeholders to define problems, designing data collection instruments, reporting modeling and analysis results to management and end users, and recommending data-driven solutions. The US employment and wage scope must be explained: approximately 275,600 employed in 2025, projected growth of 35% in 2025–2035 (Much faster than average), and approximately 24,800 average annual openings over ten years including replacement demand. Wage data for month 5 of 2025 show median annual wages of USD 120,230 (median hourly wages USD 57.80), with annual percentiles USD 67,240/85,660/120,230/158,880/199,130. Industries are professional, scientific and technical services 28%/finance and insurance 19%/information 11%/company and general management 10%/other industries 32%; interest code IC and preparation level Job Zone Four; also covered are mainland China's occupation-level wage gap and control points for data authorization, leakage checks, model validation, bias and drift monitoring, and domain decision review.

subject.name: Data Scientists
subject.summary: Data scientists in the United States correspond to O*NET-SOC 15-2051.00 (Data Scientists), developing and implementing techniques or analytical applications using data-oriented programming languages and visualization software to turn raw data into meaningful information. They apply data mining, data modeling, natural language processing and machine learning to extract and analyze information from large structured and unstructured datasets; use statistical software to analyze, process and clean large datasets; create charts and other visualizations to communicate analytical results; test, validate and redesign models to ensure accurate prediction of target outcomes; compare statistical model performance metrics such as loss functions or the proportion of variance explained; apply feature selection algorithms; identify relationships, trends or factors that may affect research outcomes; write new functions or applications in programming languages for analysis; read scientific articles and conference papers to identify emerging analytical trends and technologies; interview stakeholders to identify problems to analyze; design surveys or data collection instruments; report modeling and analysis results orally or in writing to management and other end users; and recommend data-driven solutions to key stakeholders. They may also create dynamic data reports. The preparation level is Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed, SVP 7.0 to below 8.0); the official education survey shows that among new entrants, 48% require a bachelor's degree, 44% a master's degree, and 4% an associate's or other two-year degree. On O*NET, tasks, work context and preparation level use this detailed occupation's own scope; its national wage page publishes annual and hourly percentiles for 2025. Comparable Chinese roles are commonly data analysis, algorithm or modeling positions; duties, employment and pay definitions do not correspond one-to-one with this US detailed occupation and cannot be interchanged.
